prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms opened frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B046 as a single prize part with Katori and Ye, and the chair's questions sharpen rather than change my reasoning. On overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes: the comb made optical frequencies countable and the single-ion work showed that one quantum system can be controlled to extreme precision. Neither contains the step that defines this entry, namely that many neutral atoms can be held in an optical lattice at a wavelength where the light shift cancels on the clock transition, with Lamb-Dicke confinement removing motional effects. That step is what allows parallel interrogation and the stability gain over ion clocks, and it is why the field reached the 10^-18 regime across several species and laboratories. On maturity: agreement between independent clocks at that level is direct experimental verification, and I do not think our judgement should be scheduled by the metrological bodies that will decide on the second. On credit: the proposal and first strontium lattice clock (Katori) and the record accuracy and many-body clock work (Ye) are separable, decisive contributions with clear owners, and I would let the citation name the invention (magic-wavelength lattice clocks) so that it is not read as a general prize for optical clocks. I weigh this as a finished, verified result with a precise origin, while accepting that it is a judgement about novelty against earlier prizes on which colleagues can reasonably differ.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection is not frivolous. A reader who sees a line running from the comb to ion clocks to lattice clocks may conclude that the committee is honouring the same programme a third time, and Danielsson and Mehlig press the point that a new organising concept in condensed matter should rank above a record-setting instrument. If the committee judges that the magic-wavelength idea is a refinement within precision spectroscopy and not a new invention, B046 loses its main support. The redefinition of the second is still pending, and while I would not wait for it, it would be reasonable for a colleague to want the committee to see it concluded. Finally, I cannot rule out from the supplied record that Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Paris and PTB groups contributed decisively enough to make two names look incomplete, and I am recalling achieved uncertainties from memory rather than from verified numbers.

responses.point: Ulf Danielsson argued that the lattice clock is a better way of making one measurement and not a new observation about nature, and that a result which changed our understanding of electronic phases should come first.
responses.response: I take the discovery versus engineering distinction seriously, but I do not think it separates these two entries as cleanly as you suggest. The magic-wavelength condition is an insight about how an atom's internal and motional degrees of freedom couple to a trapping field, and it is what makes neutral-atom ensembles usable as a frequency reference. The same instrument is now used for questions about nature: comparisons that bound variation of constants and dark-sector couplings, and the many-body physics of the clock itself. I also note that your own stated worry about B038 is attribution, and the HgTe proposers are outside the credited trio. I will not claim B046 is the more profound idea, but I still hold that it is the more complete and cleanly credited achievement. I have not changed my first choice.

responses.point: Bernhard Mehlig weighs a new organising concept above a record-setting instrument when the instrument's lineage was recently recognised, while accepting that this is a judgement about prize philosophy.
responses.response: I appreciate that you frame this as philosophy and not an objective ranking, because that is what it is. My difference is that I do not see the lattice clock as only a record. It required a concept, magic-wavelength trapping, that was not in the comb or ion-control prizes, and that concept is what the later records rest on. On B038, the Z2 classification is beautiful and I would not oppose it, but the credit gap around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the need to distinguish it from the 2016 topological-phases prize mean the committee would be arguing the citation wording as much as the science. I would rather award the entry whose credit chain we can state without footnotes.

responses.point: Olle Eriksson prefers B042 as a falsifiable prediction followed by clean experimental confirmation, with reproduction across independent groups and moire families making the field secure even though the pairing mechanism is unsettled.
responses.response: I accept the structure you describe, since a precise prediction and an experimental confirmation is what I look for as well, and B046 has it in the same form: a concept with a precise origin followed by an experiment and then independent confirmation by direct comparison. Where I remain more cautious is that in B042 the confirmation leaves the central physical question open, namely why the system superconducts, and credit to Cao, Fatemi and the earlier continuum-model authors sits outside three names. A narrow citation on flat bands and observed correlated states would answer part of that, but I would be more comfortable after a few more years, and I do not regard that as a judgement against the field.

responses.point: Goran Johansson moved from circuit QED to B046, accepts a two-name prize as defensible, and says he will not insist on B006 this year because he cannot be a neutral judge of proximity to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about your own vantage point and I agree that the proximity argument for patience on B006 is a real one. I also take your point that the 2025 prize was physically distinct from cavity-QED architecture. My remaining difficulty with B006 is practical and not about its merit: four names for three places, with the exclusion of Girvin or Blais not resolved by the supplied record. That is a harder problem than anything left on B046, and it is why I do not rank it as an alternative to my preferred configuration. Your readiness to move from sixth to first on B046 also shows that the case does not depend only on the atomic-physics colleagues.

responses.point: Mark Pearce, as chair, agreed with the two-name configuration but said he would rank B009 below B038 or B042 as a second choice because of the five-name credit set and the 2001 lineage.
responses.response: That criticism of B009 is fair and I accept it. Five names cannot be reduced to three without an arbitrary exclusion, and the condensate lineage from 2001 is a real overlap. I keep B009 as my second alternative only because it is the closest atomic-physics fallback if the committee prefers a different area in this field, and I recognise it is weaker than B038 on allocation. On your question whether the citation should separate concept from realization, I would keep one part and name the invention in the citation, since the proposal alone would not be a clock and the record performance alone would not exist without it.

responses.point: Eva Olsson supports the two-name credit but notes that my own round-1 mention of Lemonde, Takamoto and others makes the attribution a live question, and wants the citation to name the invention so it does not read as a general prize for optical clocks.
responses.response: I accept the criticism that raising other names without resolving them leaves my position loose. My resolution is that the early strontium lattice work by other groups refined and confirmed the method but did not supply the proposal or the sustained accuracy programme, so I would not widen the prize, and I recognise that I am relying on recollection for the early priority record. I fully agree on the citation, which should name magic-wavelength lattice clocks, and I have written mine accordingly. Your point about not simply rotating toward the quantum-technology community after 2025 is a fair check, and I think the lattice clock passes it because it comes from precision measurement and not from the superconducting-circuit line.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes; this is the main point on which I could be wrong.

Whether the unrecognised early strontium lattice contributions (Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto and the Paris, PTB and Boulder groups) make a two-name credit look incomplete; I rely on recollection of the history and of achieved uncertainties, not verified figures.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay the prize; I would not wait, but I accept that this is a judgement about timing.
How much a conceptual-novelty criterion should count against an instrument-level invention, where Danielsson and Mehlig reasonably weigh it more than I do.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my profile records a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Jun Ye's group is at JILA in Boulder. No collaboration, supervision or personal relationship with Ye or Katori is documented, and I do not claim one. I also work in laser spectroscopy and coherent light-matter interaction, which gives me a field bias toward atomic-physics candidates such as B046 and B009, and Lund colleagues work in neighbouring atomic physics. After reading the chair's question, my view is that this is field and community proximity and not a direct tie, but I leave the decision on recusal regarding Ye to the committee and will abide by it. I note that B046 support does not rest on my preference alone: Johansson, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce reach it independently.
